newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs attack draft EU fuel/car emission rules.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs attack draft EU fuel/car emission rules.

text.p: European Commission proposals setting car emission and fuel quality rules beyond the year 2000 came under fire on Wednesday during the first step of their scrutiny by European parliamentarians.

Euro-MPs on the parliament's environment committee voted to beef up two Commission proposals to cut various pollutants by two thirds by 2010, one setting emission norms for petrol and diesel-engined vehicles and the other governing fuel quality.

French Green Noel Mamere and German Socialist Bernd Lange, responsible for drafting parliament's reports on the proposals, criticised the Commission for using flawed cost estimates and poor data on localised urban peaks in air pollution.
"Experience has very clearly shown that cost data provided by the industry involved can turn out to be a smokescreen...," said Lange in his report on car emissions.
Changes adopted by the committee to proposed vehicle emissions laws would make mandatory the non-binding limits set by the Commission for 2005.

It would also tighten vehicle testing procedures by including emissions testing from engine start-up and at sub-zero temperatures, two scenarios excluded from current tests but which cause significant pollution.
Another amendment would double the required durability of new vehicles' anti-pollution equipment, which would have to last for at least 160,000 kilometres (100,000 miles) or 10 years.
Adopted changes would also make it mandatory for diesel vehicles to have the same on-board, fault-detection systems as required for petrol-engined ones.
"...It cannot be right that the diesel engine is given a special exemption in respect of the durability of anti-pollution devices," Lange said.

The committee also voted to tighten in-service testing of new cars, giving authorities the power to force car makers to recall models with anti-pollution equipment which fails early on in a vehicle model's life. Such systems already exist in Sweden and the United States.

Parliamentarians also tightened up proposed rules for petrol and diesel fuels for passenger cars, slashing the proposed year-2000 limit value for sulphur in petrol to 30 parts per million (ppm) compared with the 1996 average of 300.
The committee said allowed sulphur levels in diesel should be cut even more drastically to 100 ppm in 2000, compared with 1996's 450 ppm average, and 30 ppm in 2005.
Another amendment, if it survives through to adoption, would require the Commission to draw up by the end of 1998 a directive regulating cars' emissions of carbon dioxide.
Both reports are now due for scrutiny in the parliament's full plenary session in April, which could adopt them as they are or vote for further amendments.

While changes voted through on Wednesday could be toned down again before the drafts finally become EU law, they provide pointers to the likely battle lines between national governments and the parliament in eventual head-to-head negotiation.
Parliamentary scrutiny is in parallel with EU member state negotiations, which are slated to complete their first phase in June at the earliest.
